source.title: Induction Head Toxicity Mechanistically Explains Repetition Curse in Large Language Models
source.authors: Shuxun Wang; Qingyu Yin; Chak Tou Leong; Qiang Zhang; Lin-Yi Yang

page_placements.theme: Induction-like heads in degenerate repetition and prompt echo

record.file_problem: The full paper text is present. Some tables appear flattened or incomplete in the supplied text.
record.tranche_reason: The study uses activation patching and an operational synthetic-copy task to investigate induction-head behavior and its role in repetitive generation, rather than reproducing the original training-time measurements.
record.gate_note: The study tests induction behavior with activation patching and reports results from descaling induction-head contributions during repetition. Section 2's repetition results across models and token frequencies do not measure induction heads, so they are not rows. The paper discusses in-context learning and claims descaling preserves capabilities, but does not measure loss by token index or few-shot learning.
record.test_reason: The study uses induction heads as a tool to explain and mitigate the repetition curse. It picks the top 2% of heads by logit recovery on a synthetic copy task, which finds high-recovery heads by construction. Its claim that these heads show prefix matching and copy boosting gives no numbers and no comparison with other heads. It does not measure previous-token composition, training dynamics, loss by token index or few-shot learning. Its own results concern toxicity ratios, entropy and descaling performance, not whether any version holds.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. The authors conclude that induction-head 'toxicity' (dominance over other heads' logit contributions) is a fundamental mechanism of the repetition curse. They report that logarithmic descaling of induction-head outputs mitigates repetition with near-baseline perplexity. They acknowledge that it may weaken in-context learning, and that head identification rests on synthetic copy tasks.
record.recipe_differences: Uses synthetic copy-task activation patching, toxicity ratios, and inference-time head descaling in instruct models. It does not reproduce the original training-time induction-head formation or in-context-learning loss measurements.
record.method_sensitivity: The study reports that repetition outcomes vary with token frequency and that descaling results depend on the scaling function and its c setting; it states that c = 2 works well, while small or large choices can respectively under-suppress repetition or impair in-context learning.

fits_no_version.finding: In Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct, the share of causal influence from selected copy-task heads rises sharply during repetition-512 and stays low on MMLU-Pro and ARC-Challenge. Entropy decay is 1.7 under toxicity versus 0.3 under normal conditions.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Copy-task-selected heads dominate logits during runaway token repetition in instruct LLMs.

fits_no_version.finding: Logarithmic descaling of the selected heads lets Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct follow repetition counts up to 512. Perplexity stays near baseline (2.25 vs 2.21).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Down-weighting induction-like heads at inference curbs repetition with little perplexity cost.

record.problems: The induction-head identification uses a synthetic copy task, and the authors acknowledge that it may not reflect natural repetitive text generation. The toxicity-ratio experiment is reported for Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct, while the head maps provide figure-only values. No uncertainty estimates are stated. The paper's text gives differing c settings for optimal descaling in different passages (c = 2 and c = 10); Table 2 is flattened such that its repetition-control values cannot be assigned confidently.
record.rows_left_out: Section 2's cross-model repetition and token-frequency results do not measure induction heads, so they are not rows. Table 2's flattened repetition-control values cannot be assigned reliably to its scaling-function rows. Table 3 reports perplexity for descaling configurations, not induction-head copying, in-context-learning loss by token index, or few-shot task learning.

untested.parts: Not tested. There are no small attention-only models, no previous-token head composition, and only behavioural heads in large instruct models. The authors state these heads differ from mechanistically defined ones.
No loss-by-token-index or ablation effect on in-context learning is measured.
Heads are found by top-2% selection in three instruct families. Induction behaviour is asserted, not quantified. There are no multiple training runs, other architectures or modalities.
No variation in training data or setup.
No few-shot task learning is measured.

record.verdict_notes: Labels are empty because no version is tested; the reader's V1 and V4 'supports' labels are dropped. The V1 link fails because the models are large instruct models and no composition is measured. The V4 evidence is selection by construction, with figure-only values. The paper's claims about impaired in-context learning at large c and capability preservation come with no numbers. The text is inconsistent on the optimal c (2 vs 10). No uncertainty is reported.

versions.untested_parts: The study tests behavioral copying and causal influence using larger instruct models, not composition with an earlier previous-token head in small attention-only transformers. The authors explicitly distinguish their behavioral induction heads from mechanistically defined heads in two-layer pretrained transformers.
No training-time formation window, in-context-learning transition, or training-loss bump is measured.
The study does not measure how much of loss-by-token-index in large transformers is caused by induction heads.
Induction behavior is assessed in three instruct models from different model families. The study does not test multiple training runs, other architectures, or other modalities.
The study does not vary training data or training setup to measure when induction heads form or whether in-context learning persists.
The study does not compare induction heads with other mechanisms on few-shot task learning.
The study does not examine training-time formation as a sequence of sub-steps or overlapping transitions.

rows.subject: Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct
rows.operation_detail: Activation patching on a synthetic randomized copy task to measure each attention head's causal importance.

conditions.value: systematic patching across all model layers; top 2% selected as induction heads

rows.measure: Induction causal importance I(i,j), measured by logit recovery for the correct continuation token
rows.baseline: Corrupted-forward-pass logits; clean-forward-pass logits used as the recovery reference
rows.note: The text says the top-scoring heads show prefix matching and copy boosting; the causal-importance values are presented in the heatmap.
rows.check: This is a head-selection step, not a test. Heads are ranked by copy-task logit recovery and the top 2% are taken. Values appear only in a heatmap, and induction behaviour is asserted without numbers. Not V1: these are 7B instruct models, not small attention-only transformers, and no previous-token composition is measured.

relation.reason: Induction heads serve as an operational tool for studying repetition toxicity and mitigation; selection of the top 2% by copy-task recovery does not independently test the listed claims.

tranche.reason: Uses copy-task-selected heads to explain prompted repetition and evaluate descaling; the reported outcomes do not test V1–V7.

source_check.notes: The paper internally conflicts: Section 4.4 claims accurate counts through 512, whereas Table 2 reports 118.9 for logarithmic descaling on repetition-512. PPL comes from separate general text-generation tasks; its prose specifies c=10, whereas Table 3 specifies c=2.
